newsitem.title: USA: NRC says no reason to block Salem NJ nuke restart.
newsitem.headline: NRC says no reason to block Salem NJ nuke restart.

text.p: Though final testing and evaluation have not been completed, a senior official with the Nuclear Regulatgory Commission (NRC) said Wednesday there was nothing to prevent a restart of Public Service Electric and Gas Co's (PSE&G) Salem 2 nuclear power plant.
"At this point, in our judgement is there is nothing in there that would prevent a restart," NRC regional administrator Hub Miller, told the full commission at a meeting here.
"There are no issues that I know of that are restart issues," he added.
Salem 2 and the adjacent unit Salem 1, both with a generation capacity of 1,106 megawatts (MW), have been shut since mid-1995 after the NRC raised concerns over the units' safety.
PSE&G, the Newark, N.J.-based utility subsidiary of Public Service Enterprise Group, Inc, is the operator and part owner of both nuclear units at the Salem power station.
Other owners include Philadelphia-based PECO Energy Co, Delmarva Power & Light Co, based in Wilmington, Delaware, and Atlantic Energy Inc in Egg Harbor Township, New Jersey.
Miller told Reuters after the meeting that if everything went as expected, the NRC would formally approve the restart in a letter to be issued late next week.
PSE&G officials said after the meeting that they hoped to restart the unit around July 12.
Jim Ferland, chairman of PSE&G, told Reuters that he hoped the plant would be putting power back on the grid in late July following two to three weeks of low power testing.
"We have gone at this so deliberately, we will take a few more days if necessary," Ferland said. "We think we have fixed all the things that need to be fixed."
Ferland said the extensive refurbishment of Salem unit 2 had nearly created a new plant that should operate for at least 20 more years.
"We will be paid back many times over for the care and attention and time we've given to this," he said.
Miller said that a 14-member NRC assessment team was about to finish a final inspection and that he would meet on Friday with the managers of the Salem plant.
The NRC said the Salem plant had already undergone 17,000 hours of inspection since it was closed.
